title: A solo dev spent a year and 100,000 lines of AI-written JavaScript shipping a Steam game. His take: "It's a myth that anyone can 'one prompt' a commercially viable game"
author: shaymagen
selftext:
I run Vibe1Up, a small site that lists games made with AI. This week I interviewed Twin (@TwinTowerCity on X), a solo dev with a day job who just shipped Captive 3000 on Steam. It's a real-time, grid-based sci-fi dungeon crawler in the spirit of Captive, Dungeon Master and Eye of the Beholder. His process is one of the more honest accounts of building a commercial game with AI that I've seen, so here's the short version.

**How it started**

It wasn't meant to be a commercial game. He wanted to make a simple browser-based 3D maze puzzle game for fun. After a while he realized that if he kept going, he could turn it into a real product. In his words: "I learned the steps as I went along and I had no idea what I was doing at the beginning!"

**The stack and how it changed**

\- The first \~2,000 lines were written in ChatGPT.

\- When the code outgrew that workflow, he moved to Cursor, mostly with Claude Opus.

\- The game is now about 100,000 lines of JavaScript. Along the way he built his own JS engine and a level/map designer that can be reskinned.

\- Music: Suno. Graphics: ChatGPT and OpenArt.

\- After launch, Grok Bot for marketing and admin.

\- It runs in the browser (including iPad/tablet) as well as on Steam.

**The models improved under him**

The thing that surprised him most was how much the models got better over that year: "It was so much better by the end of the year that I went back and recreated a lot of my early graphics." If you're on a long project, plan for redoing early assets once the tools catch up.

**The one-prompt myth**

When I asked him about the hardest part, he said: "Time, and credits. Pretty much anything can be created with AI but it's a myth that anyone can 'one prompt' a commercially viable game. I spent hundreds of hours working on Captive 3000 over a year and it consumed a lot of AI credits."

**His advice for a first AI-assisted game**

"Just start, even if you don't know what you're doing, you'll figure it out along the way."

The free demo is the first three levels (about three hours), and your progress carries over to the full game: https://store.steampowered.com/app/4982850

For those of you working on bigger AI-assisted projects: at what point did you outgrow chat-window coding and move to an editor like Cursor? And have you gone back to redo early assets as the models got better?

We're also giving away 3 Steam keys for Captive 3000 on X from @Vibe1Up this week.

comments.author: MiskatonicGame
comments.body: I have some game ideas that I am iterating on, my biggest concern is actually how much time I need to spend on creating the business around it. Are you distributing them commercially or doing this just for the lolz?

comments.author: Jin_Sakai_Ghost
comments.body:
If one year of AI can do only this, there is no reason for AI haters to hate AI.

Honestly, either the dev didn't know how to use AI, or he is just trolling us.

replies.author: shaymagen
replies.body: Fair to not like it, but I don't think "the dev didn't know how to use AI" is really fair. Twin built the whole thing solo on his own custom JS engine and actually shipped it on Steam, which most people never get to. It's a first release, not the best AI can do. Feedback on what feels off would probably help him more 🙂

replies.author: Jin_Sakai_Ghost
replies.body:
I am not criticizing the game, I am criticizing the use of 'one year' and '100,000 lines' phrases to describe the game.

No one can make a commercially viable game from one-prompting. But, to tell that, using phrases like 'one year of AI' and '100,000 lines of code' is wrong by several counts.

replies.author: shaymagen
replies.body: Fair point, and I agree nobody one-prompts a real game. That's kind of the point though, it wasn't one prompt. Those numbers came from the dev himself, he worked on it for about a year with AI as his main tool. The line count was just meant to show how much work went into it, not that it makes the game good. Appreciate the honest take 🙂
